opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that DNA is the instruction manual, but proteins are the machines that actually do the work in your cells. Your genome tells you the sequence of amino acids, essentially a long string of letters, but that string doesn't do anything on its own. It folds up into a very specific three-dimensional shape, and it's that shape that determines what the protein does. Whether it's an enzyme cutting another molecule, a receptor sitting in a cell membrane waiting for a signal, or an antibody grabbing onto a virus, the function comes from the geometry.

So there's this gap. We've become extraordinarily good at reading sequences. Sequencing is cheap and fast, and we have hundreds of millions of protein sequences. But determining the structure experimentally, through X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy or NMR, has historically been slow, expensive and sometimes just doesn't work for a given protein. You might spend a year or more, sometimes an entire PhD, on a single structure.

If you can bridge that gap computationally, going straight from sequence to structure, you change the economics of a lot of biology. Someone studying a disease can look at a mutation and ask, "Where does this sit on the protein? Is it in the active site? Does it break the fold?" Someone designing a drug can reason about where a molecule might bind. It turns structure from a scarce, hard-won resource into something you can just look up.

There's also a scientific beauty to it. The fact that the sequence alone largely determines the structure has been known for decades, so in principle the information is all there. The question was always whether we could learn to read it. That's what made it such a compelling problem: well defined, deeply important, and for a long time very stubbornly unsolved.

r001.rationale: The response says the amino-acid sequence folds into a specific three-dimensional shape, but does not communicate that the shape is compact.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the shape determines protein function and gives examples of functions tied to that geometry.

r003.rationale: It contrasts cheap, fast sequencing with experimental structure determination that is slow, expensive, and may not work for a given protein.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I usually put it is that DNA is really the only part of biology we can read cheaply and at scale. Sequencing has gotten absurdly good, so we have this enormous flood of genetic information, and most of what it encodes is instructions for making proteins. But the sequence by itself is almost like a parts list without a diagram. A protein is a string of amino acids, and that string folds up into a very specific three-dimensional shape, and it's the shape that does the work. It's the shape that lets an enzyme grab onto one molecule and not another, or lets a signaling protein dock with its partner, or lets an antibody recognize a virus.

So if you want to go from "here is the gene" to "here is what this thing actually does in the cell," structure is the bridge. And historically that bridge was incredibly expensive to build. Experimental methods like X-ray crystallography or cryo-EM can take months or years for a single protein, and plenty of proteins simply refuse to cooperate. So we ended up in this strange situation where we knew hundreds of millions of sequences and had structures for a tiny fraction of them.

The other thing that makes it central, and honestly what drew me to it, is that it's one of the few problems in biology where the question is so cleanly posed. The information is all there in principle. Anfinsen showed decades ago that for many proteins the sequence determines the fold. So it's not a question of missing data, it's a question of understanding the mapping. And that made it feel tractable in a way that a lot of biology doesn't, while still being a problem where getting it right unlocks an enormous amount of downstream science, from understanding disease mutations to designing new drugs and new enzymes.

r001.rationale: It says the amino-acid string folds into a specific three-dimensional shape, but does not describe that shape as compact.

r002.rationale: It directly connects the protein’s shape to its work, giving examples of enzymes binding molecules and antibodies recognizing viruses.

r003.rationale: It contrasts cheap, large-scale DNA sequencing with experimental structure determination that can take months or years for one protein.

astra-6.text:
Well, DNA gives you the instructions for making a protein—more directly, its sequence of amino acids. But that sequence doesn’t immediately tell you how the protein works. The chain folds into a three-dimensional shape, and that shape is a huge part of what allows it to do something: catalyse a reaction, recognise another molecule, or carry a signal across a cell membrane.

So you have this extraordinary resource in sequencing. We can read the instructions for biology at enormous scale. But there’s a gap between reading those instructions and understanding the machinery they produce. Predicting structure helps bridge that gap.

It doesn’t solve all of biology. Proteins move, they interact, and their behaviour depends on their environment. But a structure gives you something concrete to reason about. You can start asking why a mutation might disrupt a protein, how it recognises a binding partner, or what experiment would help you understand its function. That makes it a starting point for a tremendous amount of biological discovery.

r001.rationale: The response says the protein chain folds into a three-dimensional shape, but it does not describe that shape as compact.

r002.rationale: It connects the folded three-dimensional shape to what a protein can do, giving examples such as catalysing a reaction and recognising another molecule.

r003.rationale: It says DNA instructions can be read at enormous scale and describes a gap in understanding, but does not state that determining even one protein’s structure is difficult.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, DNA tells you the sequence of a protein—the order of its amino acids—but it doesn’t directly tell you how that chain folds into a three-dimensional shape. And that shape is central to how the protein works: what it binds to, what reactions it can carry out, how it interacts with other molecules in the cell.

So you have this enormous amount of information that we can read from genomes, and the question is how to turn it into an understanding of biology. Structure gives you a really powerful bridge between the sequence and what the molecule actually does. It can help you understand why a mutation causes a problem, or how you might design an experiment to investigate a protein’s function.

It’s not the whole story—proteins move, they interact, and they operate in a very complicated environment—but knowing the structure gives you a much better starting point for asking those questions.

r001.rationale: It says the amino-acid chain folds into a three-dimensional shape, but does not describe that shape as compact.

r002.rationale: It connects shape to function by explaining that shape determines what a protein binds, what reactions it carries out, and how it interacts with other molecules.

r003.rationale: It says DNA reveals the amino-acid sequence but does not state that determining a protein’s structure is difficult, even for a single protein.
